title: Chain-of-Thought Oversight Requires Separate Evidence for Faithfulness and Monitorability
claim: Evidence that a property is internally present and causally relevant does not imply an external monitor can detect the behavior.
layout: 4 bar-chart panels in one row; consistent color coding, baseline lines
description: A single row of four bar-chart panels titled (a) Decodability, (b) Causal evidence, (c) Monitorability, (d) Human agreement. Panel (a) shows grouped green (probe) and gray (text-only) bars of mean cross-validated AUC for Identify, Trace and Assess, all between 0.84 and 0.98 and nearly equal. Panel (b) shows green bars for the share of cases affected by ablating the probe direction (25.4% verdict changed, 48.1% step removed), with gray dots and a dash marking random-direction ablations and p-values above. Panels (c) and (d) use orange bars with error bars for three models (14B, 32B, 70B). In (c), jury exact accuracy falls at or below a black majority-baseline line. In (d), jury Cohen's kappa sits far below a black human-expert line with a gray CI band. Green marks the internal evidence and orange marks the monitor evidence, so the contrast between them draws the eye.
caption: Security vulnerability reasoning. Reasoning-step content is recoverable from activations, and intervention on a decoded direction affects model outputs. However, the tested jury shows limited exact-accuracy monitoring despite access to the task, trace, final answer, and reference answer. (a) The presence of three reasoning steps is recoverable from activations, but a text-only classifier on the same spans performs comparably. (b) Ablating the vulnerability-identification probe direction changes more verdicts (n = 59) and removes the identification step more often (n = 27) than random directions (dash marks their mean). (c) For all three models, the jury’s exact-accuracy point estimate lies below the majority baseline (always CORRECT). (d) The jury’s agreement with human labels (Cohen’s κ) is below the agreement between two human annotators, measured on the 14B responses (shaded: 95% CI). Error bars are 95% bootstrap CIs. 14B, 32B, and 70B denote DeepSeek-14B, QwQ-32B, and DeepSeek-70B (59, 54, 58).
abstract: A common assumption in chain-of-thought (CoT) oversight is that a visible reasoning trace makes model behavior easier to monitor. We argue that this assumption can conflate distinct properties along a chain linking a model's internal computation, reasoning artifacts, outputs, and monitor judgments. We identify four properties along this chain: reasoning visibility (whether a trace is accessible), mechanistic faithfulness (whether a trace reflects internal computation), mechanistic localizability (whether a compact causal mechanism can be isolated), and behavioral monitorability (whether a monitor can detect the target behavior). Two complementary case studies across three open-weight reasoning models show why these distinctions matter. In the security vulnerability reasoning study, probes and activation ablations provide evidence of internal representation and causal influence, but a monitor with access to the reference answer does not outperform the majority-class baseline in a held-out test. In authority-hint factual reasoning study, a monitor correctly distinguishes changed from unchanged answers, but seven mechanistic analyses do not isolate a compact causal mechanism. These results show that evidence for one claim does not establish the others. We therefore propose an evidential-chain reporting standard. Each claim carries a licensing statement that specifies its target property, access tier, and artifact, and labels each required link as supported, unsupported, or assumed. These assessments determine whether the conclusion is licensed, conditionally licensed, or not licensed.
